idiom_name: std::unordered_map<std::string, std::function<void(const Message&)>> published with atomic shared_ptr store
implementation_notes: The rule base is a keyed table of std::function destinations, and std::shared_ptr<const Table> plus the std::atomic_load/atomic_store free functions (or a mutex) publishes a whole new table atomically, so a message keeps the generation it started with. std::function accepts any callable destination - free function, lambda, member function through bind - at the cost of a possible allocation per stored target. Keep the classic structure when destinations are polymorphic services and the rules change without a rebuild; a plain switch is preferable when the rule set is compile-time constant.
pitfalls: std::atomic_load on a shared_ptr needs the <memory> free-function overloads (or a mutex): mixing them with a plain assignment of the same pointer is a data race.
A destination lambda that allocates does not fit std::function's small-object buffer, so every rule publish becomes a heap allocation and every dispatch a cache miss.
Releasing the snapshot while a message is still dispatching on that table destroys the callables mid-flight; hold it for the duration of the message.

variants.name: std::variant message model + std::visit overload set
variants.idiom_name: std::variant<...> messages dispatched with std::visit over a runtime rule table
variants.implementation_notes: When the message model is closed, the routing decision can be a std::visit over a std::variant with an overloaded visitor, which compiles to an inlined jump table with no virtual dispatch and no allocation; routing stays dynamic by having the visitor consult a runtime rule object (a keyed table or array of handlers) that is rebuilt and swapped on publish. Choose this when message types are fixed at compile time and only the mapping changes - adding a message type is a rebuild, not a rule edit - and prefer it where dispatch latency and allocation behaviour matter.
pitfalls: A generic-lambda visitor loses the compile-time exhaustiveness check that an overload set gives: a variant alternative added later then compiles silently into the wrong branch.
Capturing the rule table by value in the visitor copies it per message; hold a reference or const pointer.
A valueless-by-exception variant makes std::visit throw bad_variant_access, which a routing path that assumes noexcept will not expect.
